{{Short description|Shorthand used in statistics}}
{{More citations needed|date=September 2023}}{{use dmy dates|date=September 2025}}
[[File:Empirical rule histogram.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|For an approximately [[normal distribution|normal data set]], the values within one standard deviation of the mean account for about 68% of the set; while within two standard deviations account for about 95%; and within three standard deviations account for about 99.7%. Shown percentages are rounded theoretical probabilities intended only to approximate the empirical data derived from a normal population.]]
[[File:Standard score and prediction interval.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|right|Prediction interval (on the [[y-axis|{{mvar|y}}-axis]]) given from the [[standard score]] (on the [[x-axis|{{mvar|x}}-axis]]). The {{mvar|y}}-axis is scaled as the negative logarithm of the complement of the probability to 1, i.e. {{math|-log (1 - ''p'') ,}} and labeled with the values of {{mvar|p}}.]]

In [[statistics]], the '''68–95–99.7 rule''', also known as the '''empirical rule''' or '''68–95–99.7 rule for a normal distribution'''<ref>{{cite book|author1=Peter Westfall |author2= Kevin S. S. Henning|title=Understanding Advanced Statistical Methods|date=April 9, 2013|chapter=Chapter 9 Functions of Random Variables: Their Distributions and Expected Values|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Xj3SBQAAQBAJ&dq=68%E2%80%9395%E2%80%9399.7+rule&pg=PA243|publisher=[[CRC Press]]|location=[[Texas Tech University]]|page=243|isbn=9781466512115|quote=Some statistical sources call the 68–95–99.7 rule the ''empirical rule'' since empirical (or observed) data sets often follow these percentages. However, only data sets that look as if produced by a normal distribution will obey these percentages, so it's safer to call this rule the ''68–95–99.7 rule for a normal distribution''}}</ref> and sometimes abbreviated '''3{{sc|sr}}''' or {{nobr|'''{{math|3 ''σ''}}''',}} is a shorthand used to remember the percentage of values that lie within an [[interval estimate]] in a [[normal distribution]]: approximately 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of the values lie within one, two, and three [[standard deviation]]s of the [[Arithmetic mean|mean]], respectively.

In mathematical notation, these facts can be expressed as follows, where {{math|Pr()}} is the [[probability distribution|probability function]],<ref>{{cite book |last=Huber |first=Franz |year=2018|chapter=Chapter 5 Probability <small><small>5.1 THE PROBABILITY CALCULUS</small></small>|title=A Logical Introduction to Probability and Induction |location=New York, NY |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |page=80 |isbn=9780190845414 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z2J7DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA80 |via=Google }}</ref> {{mvar|[[Χ]]}} is an observation from a normally distributed [[random variable]], {{mvar|[[μ]]}} (mu) is the mean of the distribution, and {{mvar|[[σ]]}} (sigma) is its standard deviation:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \Pr(\mu-1\sigma \le X \le \mu+1\sigma) & \approx 68.27\% \\
  \Pr(\mu-2\sigma \le X \le \mu+2\sigma) & \approx 95.45\% \\
  \Pr(\mu-3\sigma \le X \le \mu+3\sigma) & \approx 99.73\%
\end{align}</math>

The usefulness of this heuristic depends especially on the question under consideration and the manner in which the data have been collected; most particularly the heuristic depends on the data genuinely being [[normal distribution|normally distributed]]: Among the many bell-shaped distributions often seen in real-life data, the normal distribution has notoriously "[[thin-tailed distribution|thin tails]]" – an unusual concentration of probability near its center. If the datum {{mvar|X}} is instead governed by one of the many similar-appearing and [[Student's t-distribution|commonly encountered distributions]] that have "[[fat-tailed distribution|fatter tails]]" – with probability more spread-out – the significance would be lower for all three deviations from the mean. 

{{anchor|Three-sigma rule}}In the [[empirical science]]s, the so-called '''three-sigma rule of thumb''' (or {{nobr|'''3 {{mvar|σ}} rule''')}} expresses a conventional [[heuristic]] that nearly all values are taken to lie within three standard deviations of the mean, and thus it is empirically useful to treat 99.7% [[probability]] as near certainty.<ref>This use of the phrase "three-sigma rule" became common in the 2000s, e.g. cited in
* {{cite book |title=Schaum's Outline of Business Statistics |year=2003 |publisher=McGraw Hill Professional |page=359 |isbn=9780071398763 |url=https://archive.org/details/businessstatisti0000unse |url-access=registration |postscript=none }}
* {{cite book |first=Erik W. |last=Grafarend |year=2006 |title=Linear and Nonlinear Models: Fixed effects, random effects, and mixed models |publisher=Walter de Gruyter |isbn=9783110162165 |url=https://archive.org/details/linearnonlinearm00wgra |url-access=limited |page=[https://archive.org/details/linearnonlinearm00wgra/page/n573 553] }}</ref>

In the [[social sciences]], a result may be considered [[Statistical significance|statistically significant]] (clear enough to warrant closer examination) if its [[confidence level]] is of the order of a two-sigma effect (95%), while in [[particle physics]], there is a convention of requiring statistical significance of a five-sigma effect (99.99994% confidence) to qualify as a [[Discovery (observation)|discovery]].<ref>{{cite arXiv |first=Louis |last=Lyons |date = 7 October 2013 |title=Discovering the sigificance {{nobr|of {{math|5 ''σ''}}}} |class=physics.data-an |eprint=1310.1284 }}</ref>

A weaker three-sigma rule can be derived from [[Chebyshev's inequality]], stating that even for non-normally distributed variables, at least 88.8% of cases should fall within properly calculated three-sigma intervals. For [[Unimodality#Unimodal probability distribution|unimodal distributions]], the probability of being within three-sigma is at least 95% by the [[Vysochanskij–Petunin inequality]]. There may be certain assumptions for a distribution that force this probability to be at least 98%.<ref>See:
* {{cite book |first1=D.J. |last1=Wheeler |first2=D.S. |last2=Chambers |year=1992 |title=Understanding Statistical Process Control |publisher=SPC Press |isbn=9780945320135 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XvMJAQAAMAAJ |via=Google }}
* {{cite book |first1=Veronica |last1=Czitrom |author-link= Veronica Czitrom |first2=Patrick D. |last2=Spagon |year=1997 |title=Statistical Case Studies for Industrial Process Improvement |publisher=[[SIAM]] |page=342 |isbn=9780898713947 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gEpkYxwDbvgC&pg=PA342 |via=Google }}
* {{cite journal |first=F. |last=Pukelsheim |year=1994 |title=The Three Sigma rule |journal=[[American Statistician]] |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=88–91 |doi=10.2307/2684253 |jstor=2684253 }}
<!--Czitrom has "more than 98.2%", but the article lacks presentation of what the exact assumptions are, and what exactly is a "properly constructed sigma interval" for a non-normal distribution.-->
</ref>

== Proof ==
We have that 
<math display="block">\begin{align}\Pr(\mu -n\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + n\sigma) = \int_{\mu-n\sigma}^{\mu + n\sigma} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi} \sigma} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2} dx, \end{align}</math>
doing the [[Integration by substitution|change of variable]] in terms of the [[standard score]]  <math> z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}</math>, we have
<math display="block">\begin{align}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-n}^{n} e^{-\frac{z^2}{2}}dz\end{align},</math>
and this integral is independent of <math>\mu</math> and <math>\sigma</math>. We only need to calculate each integral for the cases <math>n = 1,2,3</math>.
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\Pr(\mu -1\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 1\sigma) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-1}^{1} e^{-\frac{z^2}{2}}dz \approx 0.6826894921 \\
\Pr(\mu -2\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 2\sigma) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-2}^{2} e^{-\frac{z^2}{2}}dz \approx 0.9544997361 \\
\Pr(\mu -3\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 3\sigma) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-3}^{3} e^{-\frac{z^2}{2}}dz \approx 0.9973002039.
\end{align}</math>

== Cumulative distribution function ==
{{main|Prediction interval#Known mean, known variance}}

[[File:Cumulative distribution function for normal distribution, mean 0 and sd 1.png|270px|thumb|Diagram showing the [[cumulative distribution function]] for the normal distribution with mean ({{mvar|μ}}) 0 and variance ({{math|{{var|σ}}{{sup|2}}}})&nbsp;1]]

These numerical values "68%, 95%, 99.7%" come from the [[Normal distribution#Cumulative distribution function|cumulative distribution function of the normal distribution]].

The [[prediction interval]] for any [[standard score]] ''z'' corresponds numerically to {{math|1=(1 − (1 − <span style="font-size:100%;">{{var|Φ}}</span>{{sub|{{var|μ}},{{var|σ}}{{sup|2}}}}(z)) · 2)}}.

For example, {{math|Φ(2) ≈ 0.9772}}, or {{math|Pr({{var|X}} ≤ {{var|μ}} + 2{{var|σ}}) ≈ 0.9772}}, corresponding to a prediction interval of {{math|1 = (1&nbsp;−&nbsp;(1&nbsp;−&nbsp;0.97725)·2) =&nbsp;0.9545 =&nbsp;95.45%}}.
This is not a symmetrical interval – this is merely the probability that an observation is less than {{math|{{var|μ}} + 2{{var|σ}}}}. To compute the probability that an observation is within two standard deviations of the mean (small differences due to rounding):
<math display="block">\Pr(\mu-2\sigma \le X \le \mu+2\sigma)
 = \Phi(2) - \Phi(-2)
 \approx 0.9772 - (1 - 0.9772)
 \approx 0.9545
</math>

This is related to [[confidence interval]] as used in statistics: <math>\bar{X} \pm 2\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}</math> is approximately a 95% confidence interval when <math>\bar{X}</math> is the average of a sample of size <math>n</math>.

== Normality tests ==
{{Main|Normality test}}
The "68–95–99.7 rule" is often used to quickly get a rough probability estimate of something, given its standard deviation, if the population is assumed to be normal.  It is also used as a simple test for [[outliers]] if the population is assumed normal, and as a [[normality test]] if the population is potentially not normal.

To pass from a sample to a number of standard deviations, one first computes the [[deviation (statistics)|deviation]], either the [[Errors and residuals in statistics|error or residual]] depending on whether one knows the population mean or only estimates it.  The next step is [[standardizing]] (dividing by the population standard deviation), if the population parameters are known, or [[studentizing]] (dividing by an estimate of the standard deviation), if the parameters are unknown and only estimated.

To use as a test for outliers or a normality test, one computes the size of deviations in terms of standard deviations, and compares this to expected frequency. Given a sample set, one can compute the [[studentized residual]]s and compare these to the expected frequency: points that fall more than 3 standard deviations from the norm are likely outliers (unless the [[sample size]] is significantly large, by which point one expects a sample this extreme), and if there are many points more than 3 standard deviations from the norm, one likely has reason to question the assumed normality of the distribution. This holds ever more strongly for moves of 4 or more standard deviations.

One can compute more precisely, approximating the number of extreme moves of a given magnitude or greater by a [[Poisson distribution]], but simply, if one has multiple 4 standard deviation moves in a sample of size 1,000, one has strong reason to consider these outliers or question the assumed normality of the distribution.

For example, a 6''σ'' event corresponds to a chance of about two [[parts per billion]]. For illustration, if events are taken to occur daily, this would correspond to an event expected every 1.4 million years.  This gives a [[normality test#Back of the envelope test|simple normality test]]: if one witnesses a 6''σ'' in daily data and significantly fewer than 1 million years have passed, then a normal distribution most likely does not provide a good model for the magnitude or frequency of large deviations in this respect.
